> [!further-exploration] From: [[causality-orientations-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|causality-orientations-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **Topics for Future Research and Note Development**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 1. [[Autonomy-Supportive-Parenting]] — Full Developmental Model
> > **Connection to COT:** The primary developmental antecedent of autonomy orientation. A dedicated note would trace the specific parenting practices (choice provision, perspective-taking, informational feedback, minimizing control) through their longitudinal effects on orientation development, including moderators such as child temperament and cultural context.
> > **Priority:** High — directly instantiates COT's developmental claims.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 2. [[contingent-self-esteem]] — Structure, Dynamics, and Consequences
> > **Connection to COT:** Control orientation's characteristic self-esteem pattern. A dedicated note would examine the construct's measurement (Kernis, Deci, Ryan), its relationship to ego-involvement and narcissism, its role in psychological vulnerability, and interventions targeting the shift from contingent to genuine self-esteem.
> > **Priority:** High — one of COT's most consequential predictions.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 3. [[Need-Frustration-Theory]] — From Absence to Active Thwarting
> > **Connection to COT:** The Vansteenkiste & Ryan (2013) distinction between need satisfaction absence and active need frustration has implications for understanding the developmental pathways to control and impersonal orientations. Active frustration (controlling environments, rejecting relationships) drives orientation development more powerfully than passive absence.
> > **Priority:** Medium-High — extends COT's developmental account.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 4. [[motivational-interviewing]] — SDT-Grounded Mechanisms
> > **Connection to COT:** MI's effectiveness can be understood through COT as an orientation-development intervention. A dedicated note would trace the specific mechanisms through which MI techniques support the shift from control or impersonal orientation toward more autonomous functioning.
> > **Priority:** Medium — important applied connection.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 5. [[Cross-Cultural-Motivation-Research]] — SDT's Universality Claims
> > **Connection to COT:** The cultural boundary conditions of COT's three-orientation structure require dedicated exploration. This note would examine the evidence for and against universality, the role of cultural self-construal, and proposals for culturally contextualizing SDT constructs.
> > **Priority:** Medium — methodologically and theoretically important.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 6. [[Motivational-Affordance-Theory]] — From Ecological to Motivational Psychology
> > **Connection to COT:** The affordance concept, borrowed from Gibson's ecological psychology, provides COT's central mechanism but has not been fully elaborated as an independent construct. A dedicated note would trace the concept from ecological perception through motivational psychology and examine its utility as a general framework for understanding individual differences in environmental perception.
> > **Priority:** Medium — theoretical enrichment.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 7. [[Ego-Depletion-and-Self-Regulation]] — SDT's Alternative Account
> > **Connection to COT:** The ego depletion controversy intersects with SDT's treatment of self-regulation. SDT proposes that autonomous regulation is less depleting than controlled regulation — a claim with direct implications for how orientation profiles influence self-regulatory capacity and vulnerability to depletion.
> > **Priority:** Medium — connects COT to hot-topic self-regulation debates.

> [!further-exploration] From: [[cognitive-evaluation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|cognitive-evaluation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **Topics for Deeper Investigation**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[organismic-integration-theory]] — The Internalization Continuum
> > CET addresses only intrinsic motivation. OIT extends the motivational analysis to the full spectrum of extrinsic regulation, from external compliance through introjected, identified, and integrated regulation. A comprehensive understanding of motivation requires both CET (why rewards undermine intrinsic motivation) and OIT (how extrinsic motivation can be progressively internalized toward autonomy).
> > **Priority:** High — direct theoretical successor to CET
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[autonomy-supportive-teaching-and-learning-environments]] — Educational Design
> > CET's most practically consequential application domain. Detailed examination of how autonomy-supportive classroom environments are designed, implemented, and sustained against institutional pressures — including the specific behavioral components identified by Reeve (2006) and the structural conditions that support or undermine autonomy-supportive practice at the institutional level.
> > **Priority:** High — primary applied domain of CET
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Flow-State-Csikszentmihalyi]] — Optimal Experience and Intrinsic Motivation
> > Csikszentmihalyi's flow concept — the state of complete absorption in an optimally challenging activity — represents a key convergent construct with CET's intrinsic motivation. Both describe internally motivated engagement that requires challenge-skill balance and absence of controlling external pressure. Examining the relationship, overlap, and distinctions between flow and CET-defined intrinsic motivation would strengthen the knowledge graph.
> > **Priority:** Medium — convergent theoretical construct
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[feedback-design]] — Informational vs. Controlling Feedback Architecture
> > CET's functional significance framework implies specific design principles for feedback systems: emphasize competence information over evaluative judgment, frame feedback as mastery-diagnostic rather than normative-comparative, deliver within autonomy-supportive contexts. A dedicated treatment of feedback design principles grounded in CET would serve as a practical reference for educational and organizational design.
> > **Priority:** High — practical application bridge
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[motivational-interviewing]] — CET Principles in Clinical Practice
> > The motivational interviewing approach (Miller & Rollnick) shares deep conceptual resonance with CET's informational versus controlling distinction. MI's emphasis on autonomy maintenance, reflective listening, and avoidance of directive pressure maps closely onto CET's prescriptions for autonomy-supportive interpersonal style. Examining this convergence would bridge CET theory with clinical practice.
> > **Priority:** Medium — cross-domain application
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[gamification]] — CET Analysis of Digital Engagement Systems
> > Modern gamification systems (points, badges, leaderboards, streaks) represent a massive real-world application of external reward contingencies to intrinsically motivating and non-motivating activities. CET provides a precise analytical framework for predicting which gamification mechanics will support versus undermine intrinsic motivation — a timely analysis given the pervasiveness of gamified digital environments.
> > **Priority:** Medium — contemporary application
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[achievement-goal-theory]] — Mastery vs. Performance Orientations
> > Achievement Goal Theory (Dweck, Nicholls, Ames) distinguishes mastery goals (focused on learning and improvement) from performance goals (focused on demonstrating ability relative to others). This distinction intersects with CET's informational/controlling axis: mastery environments are informational; performance environments are controlling. A comparative analysis would strengthen both theoretical frameworks.
> > **Priority:** High — complementary motivation theory
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Replication-Crisis-in-Psychology]] — Methodological Implications for CET
> > Given that CET's foundational experiments date to the 1970s and employed methodological practices (small samples, underpowered designs, flexible analytical strategies) now recognized as problematic, a dedicated examination of the replication status and methodological robustness of CET's empirical foundation would be valuable for epistemic calibration.
> > **Priority:** Medium — methodological context

> [!further-exploration] From: [[goal-contents-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|goal-contents-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **Topics for Deeper Investigation**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 1. [[Materialism|Materialistic Values and Consumer Culture]]
> > GCT's findings on extrinsic aspiration and well-being intersect with the broader materialism literature. A dedicated exploration could trace how consumer culture functions as an aspirational ecology promoting extrinsic goal content at societal scale, with implications for advertising regulation, consumer education, and cultural policy.
> > **Priority:** High — directly extends GCT's most practically consequential findings.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 2. [[aspiration-index|Measurement of Aspirations: Psychometric Challenges]]
> > A deep dive into the Aspiration Index's psychometric properties, cultural adaptations, alternative measurement approaches, and the ipsative vs. normative measurement debate would strengthen the methodological foundation for interpreting GCT research.
> > **Priority:** Medium — methodological foundation for critical evaluation.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 3. [[Social-Media-and-Well-being|Digital Aspiration Ecologies: Social Media and Goal Content]]
> > The intersection of GCT with digital platform design, algorithmic content curation, and social media's well-being effects represents an urgent emerging research area. How do platforms shape aspiration profiles, and can GCT-informed design principles mitigate extrinsic aspiration promotion?
> > **Priority:** High — rapidly emerging research area with significant policy implications.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 4. [[organismic-integration-theory|Goal Content and Regulatory Style: The Interaction Framework]]
> > The content-by-motive interaction identified in Section 7 deserves dedicated treatment — exploring how the *what* (goal content) and the *why* (regulatory style) jointly determine psychological outcomes, and how this interaction refines GCT's predictions.
> > **Priority:** Medium — important theoretical refinement.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 5. [[Life-Goals|Goal Content Across the Lifespan: Developmental Trajectories]]
> > An investigation of how aspiration profiles form, stabilize, and shift across developmental stages — from childhood through emerging adulthood, midlife, and aging — incorporating longitudinal evidence and developmental theoretical perspectives.
> > **Priority:** Medium — bridges GCT with developmental psychology.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 6. [[eudaimonia|Eudaimonic Well-Being and the Good Life: Philosophical Foundations]]
> > GCT's claim that intrinsic goals promote well-being while extrinsic goals do not implicitly draws on eudaimonic philosophical traditions. A dedicated exploration of the philosophical underpinnings — from Aristotle through humanistic psychology to contemporary eudaimonic science — would deepen the conceptual foundation.
> > **Priority:** High — grounds GCT in deeper philosophical tradition.

> [!further-exploration] From: [[organismic-integration-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|organismic-integration-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **Expansion Topics for Continued PKB Development**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory-BPNT|Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory-(BPNT)]]
> > *Priority: High* — The SDT mini-theory most closely connected to OIT, specifying autonomy, competence, and relatedness as universal psychological needs whose satisfaction facilitates and whose frustration impedes internalization. Deep engagement with BPNT provides the theoretical infrastructure for OIT's environmental facilitation claims.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Cognitive-Evaluation-Theory-(CET)]]
> > *Priority: High* — OIT's sibling mini-theory addressing the conditions under which external events (rewards, feedback, surveillance) enhance or diminish intrinsic motivation. Understanding CET's account of functional significance of events is essential for the complete OIT picture.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[contingent-self-worth]]
> > *Priority: High* — The psychological construct most directly related to introjected regulation. Deep engagement with the contingent self-worth literature (Kernis, Crocker, Park) provides complementary perspective on the ego-involvement mechanisms OIT's introjection construct identifies.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[motivational-interviewing]]
> > *Priority: High* — The clinical application framework most directly aligned with OIT's facilitation principles. Understanding MI's evidence base and theoretical structure provides insight into how OIT concepts are operationalized in practice.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[self-regulated-learning]]
> > *Priority: Medium* — The learning science domain most directly connected to OIT's educational applications. Systematic engagement with the SRL literature would allow integration of OIT's motivational framework with cognitive and metacognitive strategy frameworks.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Cognitive-Dissonance-Theory]]
> > *Priority: Exploratory* — Festinger's theory of attitude change through behavioral enactment has structural similarities to OIT's account of internalization through engaged activity: both posit mechanisms by which behavior under external pressure can, under appropriate conditions, produce genuine attitude/value change.

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Interdependence-Theory]] and Motivational Quality**
> > *Connection*: Interdependence theory (Kelley & Thibaut) analyzes how relational partners' outcomes depend on each other's behavioral choices and examines transformation of motivation from direct exchange to relationship-oriented concerns. Examining how interdependence theory's transformation of motivation concept maps onto RMT's autonomous/controlled distinction — and whether the two frameworks produce convergent or divergent predictions — would deepen both theories.
> > *Depth Potential*: High — both are sophisticated motivational theories of close relationships; their integration would produce a richer analysis than either provides alone.
> > *Priority*: High

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **Implicit Relationship Motivation Measures**
> > *Connection*: The absence of validated implicit RMT measures is identified in this report as a significant gap. The development and validation of Implicit Association Test (IAT) adaptations for relational motivation quality represents both a methodological and theoretical priority.
> > *Depth Potential*: High — addresses a fundamental measurement challenge and connects to the implicit/explicit motivation literature.
> > *Priority*: High

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Terror-Management-Theory]] and Relationship Motivation**
> > *Connection*: Terror Management Theory proposes that awareness of mortality generates anxiety managed through cultural worldview defense and close relationship investment for existential protection. The relationship between death-salience-activated relational motivation (which may have substantial controlled elements — the relationship as existential anxiety buffer) and autonomous relationship motivation represents an underexplored theoretical intersection.
> > *Depth Potential*: Moderate — niche intersection but theoretically interesting for understanding controlled motivation sources.
> > *Priority*: Exploratory

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Compassionate-vs-Self-Image-Goals]] in Relational Motivation**
> > *Connection*: Canevello and Crocker's distinction between compassionate goals (genuinely helping others) and self-image goals (performing helpfulness to manage self-image) maps directly onto RMT's autonomous vs. controlled motivation distinction. Their empirical work demonstrates behavioral and relational consequence differences that parallel RMT predictions.
> > *Depth Potential*: High — direct conceptual intersection with strong empirical grounding.
> > *Priority*: High

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **RMT in Non-Romantic Relationships: Friendship Quality**
> > *Connection*: Most RMT empirical work focuses on romantic relationships; the extension to deep platonic friendships, mentorship relationships, and close family bonds (particularly sibling relationships in adulthood) represents an important expansion of the theory's scope.
> > *Depth Potential*: Moderate — largely unexplored empirically; likely high theoretical applicability.
> > *Priority*: Medium

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **Positive Psychology Integration: [[Flourishing]] and Autonomous Relational Bonds**
> > *Connection*: Positive psychology's concept of flourishing (Seligman's PERMA model; Ryan & Deci's eudaimonic well-being framework) identifies close relationships as a central component of flourishing. RMT specifies *which kind* of close relationship structures contribute most to flourishing — those characterized by autonomous motivation and genuine need satisfaction. Systematic integration of RMT with the broader flourishing literature would enrich both frameworks.
> > *Depth Potential*: High — significant applied implications for positive psychology interventions, relationship coaching, and community well-being design.
> > *Priority*: High

> [!further-exploration] From: [[attribution-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-03|attribution-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]]
> **Priority Expansion Topics**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[self-regulated-learning]] and Attribution
> > **Connection:** Attribution patterns shape the deployment of self-regulated learning strategies — students with effort-strategy attributions are more likely to monitor comprehension, seek information, and adjust strategy, while ability-attributing students disengage metacognitive monitoring. A deep exploration of SRL theory would illuminate how attribution functions as an upstream variable in the full self-regulation cycle.
> > **Priority:** High
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[stereotype-threat]] and Attributional Processes
> > **Connection:** Stereotype threat — the risk of confirming a negative group stereotype through one's performance — creates attributional complexity by adding stereotype-confirmation attribution as a possible meaning of failure, amplifying self-evaluative threat. Understanding Stereotype Threat deepens the analysis of attributional ambiguity and its consequences for educational equity.
> > **Priority:** High
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[achievement-goal-theory]] (Elliot & McGregor)
> > **Connection:** Achievement goal orientation — mastery-approach, performance-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-avoidance — is both a downstream consequence of attribution patterns and an upstream predictor of new attribution formation. A comprehensive treatment of 2×2 Achievement Goal Theory would provide the systematic motivational architecture that Attribution Theory implies but does not fully develop.
> > **Priority:** High
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Cognitive-Behavioral-Therapy-Principles]] and Attributional Restructuring
> > **Connection:** CBT's cognitive restructuring component is fundamentally attributional — identifying, challenging, and revising maladaptive causal beliefs about negative life events. A deep treatment of CBT principles would extend Attribution Theory's clinical applications across the full spectrum from mildly maladaptive classroom attributions to clinical depression treatment.
> > **Priority:** Medium
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[self-determination-theory]] × Attribution: Competence and Controllability
> > **Connection:** SDT's need for competence and the SDT framework for autonomous vs. controlled motivation are deeply connected to Attribution Theory's locus and controllability dimensions. A synthesis note exploring this connection would reveal the structural overlap and productive differences between the two frameworks.
> > **Priority:** Medium
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[metacognition]] and Attributional Accuracy
> > **Connection:** Metacognitive awareness — knowing what you know and monitoring comprehension — is both influenced by and influences attribution. Students with good metacognitive skill form more accurate attributions because they have better diagnostic access to their actual understanding; conversely, maladaptive attributions can undermine metacognitive self-monitoring. A treatment of Metacognition would complete the cognitive-motivational integration.
> > **Priority:** Medium

> [!further-exploration] From: [[basic-psychological-needs-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|basic-psychological-needs-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **Expansion Topics for PKB Development**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Terror-Management-Theory]] and BPNT Comparison**
> > *Connection:* TMT (Greenberg, Solomon, Pyszczynski) proposes that much human motivation is driven by mortality salience and the management of death anxiety, offering an existential alternative to BPNT's growth-oriented account. A comparative analysis would examine: where do the two frameworks agree (both predict that threatened individuals engage in defensive, conformist, controlled behavior)? Where do they diverge (BPNT grounds defensiveness in need frustration; TMT grounds it in death anxiety)? Can the frameworks be integrated?
> > *Priority:* high
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[attachment-theory]] and BPNT Integration**
> > *Connection:* Bowlby's attachment theory and BPNT's account of the relatedness need and developmental need satisfaction history are deeply convergent frameworks that have been developed largely independently. Key integration questions: how does secure vs. insecure attachment status relate to chronic need satisfaction/frustration patterns? How do attachment working models function as developmental products of early need environments? Does adult attachment therapy work through need-supportive mechanisms?
> > *Priority:* high
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Positive-Psychology]] and BPNT Convergences and Divergences**
> > *Connection:* SDT and positive psychology (Seligman's PERMA model, flow theory, character strengths) are both frameworks for understanding human flourishing that have developed largely independently, with genuine convergences and interesting theoretical differences. A comparative synthesis would examine: where does BPNT's account of thriving overlap with PERMA? What does BPNT offer that positive psychology frameworks typically lack (specifically the dual-process model and need frustration account)?
> > *Priority:* high
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Social-Comparison-Theory]] and Need Substitution**
> > *Connection:* Festinger's social comparison theory describes the human tendency to evaluate oneself relative to comparable others. BPNT's account of need substitutes and controlled motivation helps explain why social comparison is psychologically costly: engaging in social comparison for purposes of self-evaluation is a controlled-motivational act that provides ego-protective information but does not genuinely satisfy the competence need (which requires mastery experiences) or the relatedness need (which requires genuine caring, not social status assessment).
> > *Priority:* medium
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Mindfulness]] and BPNT Synergies**
> > *Connection:* Research by Brown & Ryan (2003) established that mindfulness — nonjudgmental present-moment awareness — is associated with autonomous motivation and higher need satisfaction, and that mindfulness training enhances autonomous regulation. A comprehensive analysis would examine the theoretical mechanisms: why does mindfulness support autonomous motivation? Is mindfulness better understood as a *condition* for or a *consequence* of need satisfaction? What therapeutic implications follow from the BPNT-mindfulness intersection?
> > *Priority:* medium
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Adverse-Childhood-Experiences]] (ACE) Research and BPNT**
> > *Connection:* The ACE research program (Felitti et al., 1998 and subsequent work) documents that adverse childhood experiences — abuse, neglect, household dysfunction — have powerful, cumulative, dose-response relationships with adult health outcomes across biological, psychological, and social domains. BPNT's developmental account of need frustration and its consequences is potentially a powerful theoretical framework for understanding *why* ACEs produce their effects: the specific mechanisms through which adverse early environments translate into worse adult outcomes. Examining the ACE literature through a BPNT lens could substantially extend both frameworks.
> > *Priority:* high

> > An investigation of how aspiration profiles form, stabilize, and shift across developmental stages — from childhood through emerging adulthood, midlife, and aging — incorporating longitudinal evidence and developmental theoretical perspectives.
> > **Priority:** Medium — bridges GCT with developmental psychology.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] 6. [[eudaimonia|Eudaimonic Well-Being and the Good Life: Philosophical Foundations]]
> > GCT's claim that intrinsic goals promote well-being while extrinsic goals do not implicitly draws on eudaimonic philosophical traditions. A dedicated exploration of the philosophical underpinnings — from Aristotle through humanistic psychology to contemporary eudaimonic science — would deepen the conceptual foundation.
> > **Priority:** High — grounds GCT in deeper philosophical tradition.

> [!further-exploration] From: [[organismic-integration-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|organismic-integration-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **Expansion Topics for Continued PKB Development**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory-BPNT|Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory-(BPNT)]]
> > *Priority: High* — The SDT mini-theory most closely connected to OIT, specifying autonomy, competence, and relatedness as universal psychological needs whose satisfaction facilitates and whose frustration impedes internalization. Deep engagement with BPNT provides the theoretical infrastructure for OIT's environmental facilitation claims.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Cognitive-Evaluation-Theory-(CET)]]
> > *Priority: High* — OIT's sibling mini-theory addressing the conditions under which external events (rewards, feedback, surveillance) enhance or diminish intrinsic motivation. Understanding CET's account of functional significance of events is essential for the complete OIT picture.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[contingent-self-worth]]
> > *Priority: High* — The psychological construct most directly related to introjected regulation. Deep engagement with the contingent self-worth literature (Kernis, Crocker, Park) provides complementary perspective on the ego-involvement mechanisms OIT's introjection construct identifies.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[motivational-interviewing]]
> > *Priority: High* — The clinical application framework most directly aligned with OIT's facilitation principles. Understanding MI's evidence base and theoretical structure provides insight into how OIT concepts are operationalized in practice.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[self-regulated-learning]]
> > *Priority: Medium* — The learning science domain most directly connected to OIT's educational applications. Systematic engagement with the SRL literature would allow integration of OIT's motivational framework with cognitive and metacognitive strategy frameworks.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Cognitive-Dissonance-Theory]]
> > *Priority: Exploratory* — Festinger's theory of attitude change through behavioral enactment has structural similarities to OIT's account of internalization through engaged activity: both posit mechanisms by which behavior under external pressure can, under appropriate conditions, produce genuine attitude/value change.

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Interdependence-Theory]] and Motivational Quality**
> > *Connection*: Interdependence theory (Kelley & Thibaut) analyzes how relational partners' outcomes depend on each other's behavioral choices and examines transformation of motivation from direct exchange to relationship-oriented concerns. Examining how interdependence theory's transformation of motivation concept maps onto RMT's autonomous/controlled distinction — and whether the two frameworks produce convergent or divergent predictions — would deepen both theories.
> > *Depth Potential*: High — both are sophisticated motivational theories of close relationships; their integration would produce a richer analysis than either provides alone.
> > *Priority*: High

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **Implicit Relationship Motivation Measures**
> > *Connection*: The absence of validated implicit RMT measures is identified in this report as a significant gap. The development and validation of Implicit Association Test (IAT) adaptations for relational motivation quality represents both a methodological and theoretical priority.
> > *Depth Potential*: High — addresses a fundamental measurement challenge and connects to the implicit/explicit motivation literature.
> > *Priority*: High

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Terror-Management-Theory]] and Relationship Motivation**
> > *Connection*: Terror Management Theory proposes that awareness of mortality generates anxiety managed through cultural worldview defense and close relationship investment for existential protection. The relationship between death-salience-activated relational motivation (which may have substantial controlled elements — the relationship as existential anxiety buffer) and autonomous relationship motivation represents an underexplored theoretical intersection.
> > *Depth Potential*: Moderate — niche intersection but theoretically interesting for understanding controlled motivation sources.
> > *Priority*: Exploratory

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Compassionate-vs-Self-Image-Goals]] in Relational Motivation**
> > *Connection*: Canevello and Crocker's distinction between compassionate goals (genuinely helping others) and self-image goals (performing helpfulness to manage self-image) maps directly onto RMT's autonomous vs. controlled motivation distinction. Their empirical work demonstrates behavioral and relational consequence differences that parallel RMT predictions.
> > *Depth Potential*: High — direct conceptual intersection with strong empirical grounding.
> > *Priority*: High

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **RMT in Non-Romantic Relationships: Friendship Quality**
> > *Connection*: Most RMT empirical work focuses on romantic relationships; the extension to deep platonic friendships, mentorship relationships, and close family bonds (particularly sibling relationships in adulthood) represents an important expansion of the theory's scope.
> > *Depth Potential*: Moderate — largely unexplored empirically; likely high theoretical applicability.
> > *Priority*: Medium

> [!further-exploration] From: [[relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|relationship-motivation-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> > [!topic-idea] **Positive Psychology Integration: [[Flourishing]] and Autonomous Relational Bonds**
> > *Connection*: Positive psychology's concept of flourishing (Seligman's PERMA model; Ryan & Deci's eudaimonic well-being framework) identifies close relationships as a central component of flourishing. RMT specifies *which kind* of close relationship structures contribute most to flourishing — those characterized by autonomous motivation and genuine need satisfaction. Systematic integration of RMT with the broader flourishing literature would enrich both frameworks.
> > *Depth Potential*: High — significant applied implications for positive psychology interventions, relationship coaching, and community well-being design.
> > *Priority*: High

> [!further-exploration] From: [[self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **Related Topics for PKB Development**
> 
> The following topics are natural next nodes for deepening SDT understanding in the knowledge graph.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **1. [[self-regulated-learning]] and SDT Intersections**
> 
> **Connection**: SDL research and SDT share substantial theoretical overlap — both address the conditions for autonomous, self-directed learning. But they have somewhat different emphases (SRL focuses more on metacognitive and cognitive strategies; SDT focuses more on motivational quality). A synthesis note comparing these frameworks would be high-value.
> **Depth Potential**: Examining where the frameworks converge (autonomy as foundation for deep SRL), where they diverge (SRL has richer metacognitive theory; SDT has richer needs theory), and how they mutually illuminate each other.
> **Knowledge Graph Role**: Bridge node between motivation domain and cognitive learning domain.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **2. [[achievement-goal-theory]] vs. SDT**
> 
> **Connection**: Achievement Goal Theory (Elliot, Nicholls, Dweck) provides a parallel and partially overlapping account of mastery vs. performance motivation. Comparing the frameworks reveals what each adds: AGT focuses on *goal orientation* (toward mastery vs. performance); SDT focuses on *regulatory quality* (autonomous vs. controlled). Their prediction profiles overlap for some outcomes (mastery orientation ≈ autonomous motivation in many contexts) but diverge for others.
> **Depth Potential**: A comparative analysis note distinguishing the constructs, their measurement, and their differential predictive utility.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **3. [[motivational-interviewing]] and SDT**
> 
> **Connection**: Motivational Interviewing as a clinical technique embodies many SDT principles (autonomy support, eliciting intrinsic motivation, rolling with resistance, developing discrepancy between current behavior and expressed values). A note on the theoretical connections between MI and SDT would enrich both the clinical and the motivational theory nodes.
> **Knowledge Graph Role**: Applied connection between motivational theory and clinical/counseling practice.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **4. [[humanistic-psychology]] and SDT's Intellectual Roots**
> 
> **Connection**: SDT emerged partly from the humanistic tradition (Rogers, Maslow) while subjecting that tradition's claims to empirical scrutiny. Understanding SDT's relationship to humanistic psychology illuminates both what SDT inherits (the organismic growth tendency, unconditional positive regard, the distinction between being and having) and what it modifies (replacing Maslow's hierarchy with three universal non-hierarchical needs; subjecting Rogers' clinical propositions to experimental test).
> **Depth Potential**: Intellectual history note tracing the SDT-humanistic lineage.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **5. [[goal-contents-theory]] and Consumer Culture Critique**
> 
> **Connection**: Tim Kasser's application of GCT to materialistic values and consumer culture provides a bridge from motivational psychology to social critique. A report or note on this connection would link SDT's framework to broader questions about institutional design, advertising effects, and the sociology of well-being.
> **Knowledge Graph Role**: Bridge from psychology to social theory and political economy.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **6. [[eudaimonia]] — Philosophical Foundations**
> 
> **Connection**: SDT's well-being theory is explicitly eudaimonic. A deep-dive note on the philosophical tradition of eudaimonic ethics — from Aristotle through contemporary philosophers (Martha Nussbaum, Amartya Sen, Derek Parfit) — would provide the philosophical context that SDT's empirical program presupposes but rarely engages explicitly.
> **Knowledge Graph Role**: Bridge node between psychology (SDT) and philosophy (ethics, political philosophy, philosophy of mind).

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **7. [[attachment-theory]] and Need Satisfaction Development**
> 
> **Connection**: SDT's developmental account of how need satisfaction histories shape causality orientations shares structure with Bowlby/Ainsworth attachment theory. Both propose that early relational patterns create internal working models that shape subsequent motivation and social functioning. A comparative note would examine overlaps, divergences, and opportunities for synthesis.
> **Knowledge Graph Role**: Bridge between motivational development (SDT-COT) and developmental attachment psychology.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01|self-determination-theory-foundational-report-2026-04-01]]
> **8. [[Positive-Psychology]] vs. SDT — Complementary or Competing?**
> 
> **Connection**: SDT and Positive Psychology (Seligman's PERMA model) share the goal of understanding human flourishing but differ in their frameworks: PERMA emphasizes positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment; SDT emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness need satisfaction. A comparative analysis note would identify where they align, where they diverge, and what a synthesis might look like.
> **Knowledge Graph Role**: Positioning node within the broader well-being theory landscape.

---

## Motivational Psychology

> [!further-exploration] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> **Topics for Continued Investigation**
> 
> 

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> - **Topic**: The Undermining Effect — Replication Crisis and Reconceptualisation
>   - **Report Type**: First Principles
>   - **Description**: The original undermining effect (Deci 1971) is SDT's most famous empirical finding, but its replication record is contested. A first-principles analysis would audit the conditions under which the effect holds, examine whether it requires the SDT theoretical apparatus or can be explained by more minimal constructs (task interest, appraisal of external control), and reconstruct a more conditionally specified account of when external rewards undermine intrinsic motivation.
>   - **Priority**: High — central to SDT's empirical case

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> - **Topic**: The Competence Need — Effectance, Flow, and Challenge-Skill Balance
>   - **Report Type**: First Principles
>   - **Description**: The three SDT needs are not equally theoretically controversial — competence is the most intuitively biological-sounding (relating to effective functioning), making it the most important to examine carefully. Does the "need for competence" add explanatory power beyond the constructs of White's effectance motivation, Csikszentmihalyi's flow, and Elliot's achievement goal framework? A first-principles analysis would examine the minimal axiomatic basis required to derive the competence-need-well-being relationship.
>   - **Priority**: High — addresses the least-examined SDT need

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> - **Topic**: Autonomy and Agency — A Philosophical Dialogue
>   - **Report Type**: Socratic Dialogue
>   - **Description**: The tension between SDT's psychological construct of autonomy (experienced volition) and philosophical accounts of self-determination (Frankfurt's hierarchy of desires, Bratman's planning agency, Korsgaard's self-constitution) is productive and not fully resolved by either tradition. A Socratic dialogue would develop both positions rigorously, examining whether they are genuinely in conflict or whether they are addressing different explanatory targets.
>   - **Priority**: High — addresses the most philosophically significant open question

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> - **Topic**: SDT Across Cultures — Universality, Variation, and Cultural Psychology
>   - **Report Type**: Foundational
>   - **Description**: A comprehensive landscape map of the cross-cultural SDT literature, examining what the replications actually establish, where culturally specific findings emerge, and how SDT researchers and critics have engaged with the universality question. Would provide the detailed evidential foundation that this first-principles report's Phase II audit treats more schematically.
>   - **Priority**: High — the universality question is the most empirically contested area

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> - **Topic**: The Normative Dimension of Basic Needs — Social Justice and SDT
>   - **Report Type**: First Principles
>   - **Description**: SDT's language of "basic needs" carries normative weight: if institutions frustrate basic psychological needs, they are not merely inefficient but are perpetrating a form of harm. The dissolution of the innateness claim in this report raises the question of whether this normative argument survives — whether needs-language can be maintained as a political-normative tool even if the biological grounding is not established. A first-principles analysis of the normative dimension would examine what philosophical work the "need" concept does in SDT's implicit social critique.
>   - **Priority**: Medium — relevant for policy and advocacy applications of SDT

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> - **Topic**: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs — A First Principles Parallel Analysis
>   - **Report Type**: First Principles
>   - **Description**: Maslow's needs hierarchy is SDT's closest ancestor and most prominent rival in the popular imagination. A parallel first-principles deconstruction would allow direct comparison of what survives from each framework when the philosophical assumptions are stripped away — and would illuminate what the "needs" framing as a whole contributes and costs in motivational theorising.
>   - **Priority**: Medium — provides comparative context for SDT's theoretical choices

> [!further-exploration] From: [[achievement-goal-theory-focused-analysis-2026-03-24|achievement-goal-theory-focused-analysis-2026-03-24]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[A-focused-treatment-of-mastery-vs.-performance-goal-orientations-—-their-measure|Measurement Validity and the Achievement Goal Construct]]
> > This expansion examines the psychometric debates underlying AGT: are mastery-approach and performance-approach goals genuinely discriminable constructs, or do measures of them overlap in ways that threaten the theoretical claims? Specific issues: the Elliot-Harackiewicz controversy partly turned on measurement artifact; the 3×2 framework extension attempts to resolve discriminant validity problems by further differentiating the mastery and performance standards. This investigation would bridge motivation theory and psychometrics, with direct implications for how seriously to take the approach-avoidance asymmetry findings.
> > **Connection to This Report:** Directly evaluates the empirical foundation of the regulatory mode primacy thesis.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Dialectical Re-Examination
> > **Prerequisites:** [[achievement-goal-theory]], [[2×2-Framework]], [[Replication-Crisis-in-Psychology]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[A-deep-dive-into-the-practical-engineering-of-mastery-oriented-learning-environm|Mastery Climate Engineering: Structural Design Principles]]
> > A focused investigation of the practical engineering of mastery-oriented learning environments — moving from the abstract principles identified in Ames' TARGET framework to the specific design specifications for assessment, grouping, recognition, authority, and time structures. This expansion would operationalize the motivational climate audit protocol in this report into a comprehensive design guide.
> > **Connection to This Report:** Directly applies the Phase V implications for assessment and climate design.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites:** [[motivational-climate-design]], [[formative-assessment]], [[achievement-goal-theory]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[A-focused-analysis-of-how-COT-orientations-shape-the-SRL-cycle|Achievement Goals and the Self-Regulated Learning Cycle]]
> > A focused analysis of how the four goal types in the 2×2 framework shape the full Zimmerman SRL cycle — forethought, performance, and reflection phases. This expansion would elaborate the connection identified in Phase V of this report and provide the detailed mechanism account for how goal orientation shapes strategic processing at each phase.
> > **Connection to This Report:** Extends the Phase V discussion of SRL infrastructure and provides the mechanistic bridge between AGT and the SRL literature.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[self-regulated-learning]], [[achievement-goal-theory]], [[forethought-phase]], [[performance-phase]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[far-transfer|Transfer-Oriented Investigation: Approach-Avoidance in Organizational Motivation]]
> > A transfer-oriented expansion applying the approach-avoidance asymmetry principle directly to organizational motivation — examining how performance review systems, promotion structures, and incentive designs activate approach or avoidance regulation, and what the asymmetric consequences are for organizational learning, innovation, and psychological safety. This expansion follows the application bridge in Phase VII of this report.
> > **Connection to This Report:** Direct application of the FAR transfer principles extracted in Phase VII.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[motivational-climate-design]], [[achievement-goal-theory]], [[growth-mindset-theory]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[attribution-theory-focused-analysis-2026-03-24|attribution-theory-focused-analysis-2026-03-24]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Attribution-Retraining-Interventions]]
> > This expansion applies the theoretical architecture developed in this report to specific empirically-studied attribution retraining programs — Wilson and Linville's academic persistence interventions, Dweck's mindset programs, and clinical applications in depression treatment. The specific question: what components of existing programs address affective reorganization, and which rely solely on cognitive reattribution? This is the natural practitioner follow-up to the theoretical analysis.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Directly applies the Two-Stage Intervention Architecture and the Stability-Expectancy Lock analysis to program evaluation.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational Report (to survey the landscape) followed by Focused Analysis (on program components)
> > **Prerequisites:** [[attribution-theory]], [[growth-mindset-theory]], [[helpless-response-pattern]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[appraisal-theory]]
> > Lazarus's appraisal theory is the broader theoretical framework within which Weiner's attribution model can be situated. A focused analysis would examine the full appraisal-to-coping sequence (primary appraisal → secondary appraisal → coping) and map it onto the attribution intervention sequence. The specific question: can coping potential appraisals (Lazarus) be targeted independently of causal attributions (Weiner) to produce motivational change?
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** The structural correspondence identified in Phase IV.3 makes this a high-value expansion for understanding the theoretical architecture.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[attribution-theory]], [[motivational-psychology]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[belonging-uncertainty]]
> > This expansion examines how stability attributions operate in the social domain — specifically, how belonging uncertainty generates stable attributions for ambiguous social feedback that produce the same Stability-Expectancy Lock dynamics in social rather than achievement contexts. The connection to attribution theory is underexplored in the belonging uncertainty literature. *This is the transfer-oriented expansion: applying the Stability-Expectancy Lock mechanism to a new domain (social belonging) to generate novel predictions.*
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** FAR Transfer Principle 1 — the Stability-Expectancy Lock — applied to social attribution contexts.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[attribution-theory]], [[belonging-uncertainty]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[growth-mindset-theory]]
> > The Growth Mindset literature is the most extensively studied applied application of attribution stability, but it typically operates without explicit reference to Weiner's emotion-mediation mechanism. A focused analysis would examine what the emotion-mediation framework predicts about mindset intervention mechanisms — specifically, does mindset intervention work by changing cognitive attribution stability, or by changing the emotion generated by stable attributions, or both?
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Growth mindset is the operationalization of Weiner's stability dimension as an individual difference; Phase IV provides the mechanistic foundation for evaluating mindset intervention claims.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Dialectical Re-Examination
> > **Prerequisites:** [[attribution-theory]], [[implicit-theory-of-intelligence]], [[growth-mindset-theory]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[self-determination-theory-focused-analysis-2026-03-19|self-determination-theory-focused-analysis-2026-03-19]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[relationship-motivation-theory]]
> > RMT extends the SDT internalization analysis to close personal relationships, treating the quality of intimate connections as itself governed by the three basic needs. A deep analysis of RMT would examine how the [[perceived-partner-responsiveness]] construct operationalizes need support in dyadic contexts, and how the controlled/autonomous distinction maps onto relationship quality outcomes. The Integration Paradox has a specific form in intimate relationships — secure attachment may be both the outcome and the prerequisite of the kind of genuine mutuality that RMT posits.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[The-Motivational-Compounding-Model]]
> > The existing PKB note on motivational compounding can be read as an applied extension of the internalization account — asking how progressively more integrated regulation compounds motivationally over time. A focused analysis of the compounding model would examine whether the same environmental conditions (autonomy support, unconditional regard) that enable the introjection-to-identification transition also enable the identity-to-action compounding that the model posits.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[causality-orientations-theory]]
> > COT specifies individual-level variations in the disposition to orient toward autonomy, control, or impersonality — treating these as stable individual differences in how people tend to process their environments. A focused analysis of COT within the internalization framework would ask: does [[autonomy-orientation|autonomy orientation]] as a personality trait predispose faster or more complete internalization, or does it merely describe the outcome of sustained internalization experience?
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **SDT and the Transfer of Learning: The Motivational Conditions for Far Transfer**
> > A transfer-oriented extension of this analysis would ask: what regulatory style is required for [[far-transfer]]? The hypothesis — grounded in both SDT and transfer research — is that far transfer requires integrated regulation: the person must be able to abstract structural principles from their domain-specific application, and this kind of voluntary structural abstraction requires the generative engagement associated with autonomous motivation. Controlled motivation may produce near transfer (applying the learned procedure) but not far transfer (extracting the transferable principle).
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[The-Quality-Dimension-GCT-as-a-Theory-of-Motivational-Metabolism]]
> > This existing PKB note frames [[cognitive-evaluation-theory]] in metabolic terms. A synthesis note connecting this framing to the Internalization Metabolism Model developed in Phase VI of this report would examine whether CET (which governs intrinsic motivation) and OIT (which governs internalization) can be unified under a single metabolic framework, or whether their different concern — intrinsic motivation vs. extrinsic motivation internalization — requires different metabolic models.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **Self-Determination Theory and Organizational Culture Change: A Transfer-Domain Investigation**
> > Applying the two-phase model (autonomy restoration → internalization facilitation) and the need-frustration asymmetry to organizational culture change would constitute a genuine transfer-domain investigation. The investigation would ask: what is the organizational equivalent of conditional regard? How does organizational culture produce introjected compliance rather than integrated commitment? And what does autonomy restoration look like at the organizational level — not for individuals but for teams and divisions?

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> - **Topic**: The Normative Dimension of Basic Needs — Social Justice and SDT
>   - **Report Type**: First Principles
>   - **Description**: SDT's language of "basic needs" carries normative weight: if institutions frustrate basic psychological needs, they are not merely inefficient but are perpetrating a form of harm. The dissolution of the innateness claim in this report raises the question of whether this normative argument survives — whether needs-language can be maintained as a political-normative tool even if the biological grounding is not established. A first-principles analysis of the normative dimension would examine what philosophical work the "need" concept does in SDT's implicit social critique.
>   - **Priority**: Medium — relevant for policy and advocacy applications of SDT

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> - **Topic**: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs — A First Principles Parallel Analysis
>   - **Report Type**: First Principles
>   - **Description**: Maslow's needs hierarchy is SDT's closest ancestor and most prominent rival in the popular imagination. A parallel first-principles deconstruction would allow direct comparison of what survives from each framework when the philosophical assumptions are stripped away — and would illuminate what the "needs" framing as a whole contributes and costs in motivational theorising.
>   - **Priority**: Medium — provides comparative context for SDT's theoretical choices

> - **Topic**: The Undermining Effect — Replication Crisis and Reconceptualisation
>   - **Report Type**: First Principles
>   - **Description**: The original undermining effect (Deci 1971) is SDT's most famous empirical finding, but its replication record is contested. A first-principles analysis would audit the conditions under which the effect holds, examine whether it requires the SDT theoretical apparatus or can be explained by more minimal constructs (task interest, appraisal of external control), and reconstruct a more conditionally specified account of when external rewards undermine intrinsic motivation.
>   - **Priority**: High — central to SDT's empirical case

> - **Topic**: The Competence Need — Effectance, Flow, and Challenge-Skill Balance
>   - **Report Type**: First Principles
>   - **Description**: The three SDT needs are not equally theoretically controversial — competence is the most intuitively biological-sounding (relating to effective functioning), making it the most important to examine carefully. Does the "need for competence" add explanatory power beyond the constructs of White's effectance motivation, Csikszentmihalyi's flow, and Elliot's achievement goal framework? A first-principles analysis would examine the minimal axiomatic basis required to derive the competence-need-well-being relationship.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|self-determination-theory-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> - **Topic**: Autonomy and Agency — A Philosophical Dialogue
>   - **Report Type**: Socratic Dialogue
>   - **Description**: The tension between SDT's psychological construct of autonomy (experienced volition) and philosophical accounts of self-determination (Frankfurt's hierarchy of desires, Bratman's planning agency, Korsgaard's self-constitution) is productive and not fully resolved by either tradition. A Socratic dialogue would develop both positions rigorously, examining whether they are genuinely in conflict or whether they are addressing different explanatory targets.
>   - **Priority**: High — addresses the most philosophically significant open question

## Other / Uncategorised

> [!further-exploration] From: [[cognitive-load-theory-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-22|cognitive-load-theory-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-22]]
> **Deepening the Re-Examined CLT**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[expertise-reversal-effect]]
> > The expertise reversal effect is the empirical fulcrum on which the reconstructed CLT's expertise-indexed prescriptions rest, but it deserves a dedicated dialectical re-examination in its own right: the effect is well-established in laboratory settings with well-defined tasks, but its precise boundary conditions (how much expertise? which task types? what learning timescales?) remain incompletely mapped. The reconstructed CLT would become substantially more actionable if the expertise reversal effect were examined with the same multi-perspectival scrutiny applied here to CLT itself. Priority: **High**.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[working-memory-capacity]]
> > The WMC homogeneity assumption identified as failing in Phase III makes individual WMC differences a high-priority expansion topic. A focused examination of how WMC varies, what it predicts, and how WMC variation should modulate instructional prescriptions would provide the personalization framework that the reconstructed CLT requires but cannot currently supply. Of particular interest: the relationship between WMC and schema-mediated expertise — do WMC differences shrink as domain expertise grows? Priority: **High**.
> >
> > [!topic-idea] [[Metacognitive-Monitoring-Under-Cognitive-Load-—-When-Monitoring-is-Most-Needed-a]]
> > The bidirectional relationship between cognitive load and metacognitive monitoring warrants dedicated examination. High load degrades monitoring capacity exactly when monitoring is most needed; poor monitoring allows load to escalate unchecked. This vicious cycle has direct implications for self-regulated learning under challenging conditions and for the design of instructional environments that support both cognitive efficiency and metacognitive skill development. Priority: **Medium-High**.
> >
> > [!topic-idea] [[cognitive-theory-of-multimedia-learning]]
> > Mayer's CTML represents the most systematic extension of CLT into the design of multimedia instructional materials. The same dialectical pressure applied here to CLT would be productively applied to CTML: does CTML's twelve-principle framework inherit CLT's germane load problem? Does the expertise reversal effect apply to multimedia design in the same way it applies to conventional instruction? Does CTML account for motivational variables? A dialectical re-examination of CTML would complete the picture begun here. Priority: **Medium**.
> >
> > [!topic-idea] [[self-regulated-learning]]
> > The critical lens challenge — that CLT neglects motivational and affective variables — points directly toward the SRL integration that the reconstructed CLT needs. A synthesis examination focused specifically on how SRL frameworks (Zimmerman, Winne, Pintrich) model the motivational architecture that CLT lacks, and whether a genuine CLT-SRL integration is theoretically coherent, would represent a major advancement over both frameworks as currently specified. Priority: **Medium**.
> >
> > [!topic-idea] [[toward-an-expertise-indexed-instructional-design-principle]]
> > The reconstructed CLT in Phase V moves toward an expertise-indexed prescriptive framework but does not fully specify it. A dedicated note developing the principle that all instructional design prescriptions must specify the expertise range for which they apply — including worked examples, scaffolding, feedback density, problem variability, and assessment format — would provide the practical design guidance the reconstructed CLT promises but cannot itself deliver. Priority: **High**.

> [!further-exploration] From: [[inner-speech-vocabulary-motivation-self-efficacy-dialectical-re-examination-2026|inner-speech-vocabulary-motivation-self-efficacy-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-25]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Attribution-Retraining-Interventions]]
> > A dedicated treatment of the empirical literature on structured programs for changing attributional vocabulary and their outcomes. This expansion provides the evidence base for the constitutive vocabulary account developed here, and would deliver specific intervention protocols validated in educational contexts. Priority complement to this report.
> > **Connection to This Report:** Direct empirical foundation for Phase III's challenge; provides validated vocabulary protocols to supplement the templates in Protocol 1-3 above.
> > **Priority:** High — Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[attribution-theory]], [[bernard-weiner]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[motivational-regulation]]
> > The full landscape of motivational self-regulation strategies in academic learning — of which inner speech vocabulary is one mechanism among several. A foundational treatment would map the full toolkit and show where vocabulary development sits within it.
> > **Connection to This Report:** Provides the broader motivational regulation framework within which the vocabulary mechanism operates; prevents overextension of the vocabulary account.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites:** [[self-regulated-learning]], [[self-determination-theory]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[self-explanation-effect]]
> > The self-explanation effect (Chi et al.) shows that prompting learners to explain content aloud or in writing during reading produces comprehension gains far exceeding re-reading. The mechanism is partially the vocabulary used in the explanation — self-explanation forces the deployment of comprehension monitoring vocabulary and attributional vocabulary that operates constitutively. This expansion would examine the self-explanation effect as a vocabulary-mechanism phenomenon.
> > **Connection to This Report:** Direct application of the constitutive vocabulary account; the self-explanation effect is the self-explanation complement to the inner speech vocabulary account.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Dialectical Re-Examination (Is the self-explanation effect a comprehension phenomenon or a vocabulary-regulation phenomenon?)
> > **Prerequisites:** [[self-regulated-learning]], [[metacognitive-monitoring]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[metacognitive-scaffolding-design-patterns]]
> > How to design external prompts, templates, and reading structures that prime constructive inner speech before and during reading. The reconstructed understanding implies that scaffolds work not just by providing information but by providing constitutive vocabulary templates. This expansion would translate the vocabulary principles into scaffold design.
> > **Connection to This Report:** Direct practical extension of Phase V reconstruction and Protocol 1-3; would deliver the full design system for which this report provides the theoretical foundation.
> > **Priority:** Medium
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[metacognitive-scaffolding]], this report

> [!further-exploration] From: [[schema-theory-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-22|schema-theory-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-22]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[conceptual-change]]
> > The dialectical re-examination of schema theory repeatedly identified conceptual change theory as providing the resources schema theory itself lacks — particularly for the restructuring endpoint. A focused analysis of Posner et al.'s framework and Vosniadou's framework theory approach would constitute the necessary complement to this report: where schema theory explains comprehension within a framework, conceptual change theory explains transitions between frameworks.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report**: The reconstructed understanding's schema-disruption pedagogical inversion is partly grounded in conceptual change conditions; this node would formalize and deepen that grounding.
> > **Priority**: Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type**: Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites**: [[schema-theory]], [[cognitive-disequilibrium]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[embodied-cognition]]
> > The philosophical challenge to schema theory's representationalist assumption drew on embodied cognition research (Varela, Thompson & Rosch; Barsalou's perceptual symbol systems). A full treatment of this node would provide the foundational alternative framework that the reconstruction gestures toward but does not develop fully — particularly Barsalou's grounded cognition account and its implications for how "schemas" should be reconceived.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report**: The primary philosophical challenge target; completing this node would deepen the philosophical dimension of the reconstruction.
> > **Priority**: High
> > **Suggested Report Type**: Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites**: [[schema-theory]], [[cognitive-architecture]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[productive-failure]]
> > Manu Kapur's productive failure research program provides the empirical grounding for the schema-disruption-before-resources pedagogical prescription that emerged from this re-examination. A focused analysis would examine the specific conditions under which productive failure outperforms direct instruction, the mechanisms of its superiority, and the instructional design implications for different learning objectives.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report**: The primary empirical support for the reconstruction's pedagogical inversion; this node would constitute the empirical companion to this report's theoretical argument.
> > **Priority**: High
> > **Suggested Report Type**: Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites**: [[schema-theory]], [[conceptual-change]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[situated-learning]]
> > The situated cognition alternative framework received only abbreviated treatment in this re-examination. A foundational report on Lave & Wenger's legitimate peripheral participation model and Brown, Collins & Duguid's situated cognition perspective would deepen the "distributed schema" alternative and its implications for PKB design — particularly the question of whether a PKB can genuinely scaffold the kind of socially embedded knowledge development that situated learning theory identifies as foundational.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report**: The second alternative framework; completing this node would provide the social-cultural dimension that the reconstructed account needs.
> > **Priority**: Medium
> > **Suggested Report Type**: Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites**: [[schema-theory]], [[Scaffolding-—-Instructional-Design]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[self-determination-theory-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-19|self-determination-theory-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-19]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[undermining-effect]]
> > The meta-analytic wars between Deci/Koestner/Ryan (1999) and Cameron/Pierce (1994, 1996) constitute one of motivational psychology's most instructive empirical disputes, combining genuine methodological disagreement with substantive differences in theoretical orientation. A focused analysis would reconstruct the specific methodological choices (how "undermining" was operationalized, which studies were included vs. excluded, how moderators were handled) and draw out the general lessons about how competing meta-analyses can generate different conclusions from overlapping evidence bases. The reconstructed SDT's moderator-conditional undermining effect is only as strong as your understanding of what those moderators actually are.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[the-integration-paradox]]
> > How can a person autonomously adopt values that were initially externally imposed? This paradox is at the heart of OIT's internalization account and connects to some of philosophy's deepest puzzles about freedom, socialization, and authentic self-authorship. This report's dialectical challenge to the teleological directionality of OIT reopens rather than resolves the Integration Paradox. A focused examination would draw on Frankfurt's work on higher-order volitions, Bratman's planning theory, and Korsgaard's constitutivism to ask what philosophical resources are actually needed to ground SDT's account of internalization quality.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[causality-orientations-theory]]
> > SDT's individual differences sub-theory — distinguishing autonomy orientation (dispositional tendency toward interest-based, self-determined engagement), control orientation (dispositional tendency toward reward-contingent, approval-seeking engagement), and impersonal orientation (dispositional tendency toward amotivation and helplessness) — intersects with the practical challenge raised in Phase III in a way that deserves its own examination. Students with control or impersonal orientations do not straightforwardly benefit from autonomy-supportive environments in the way the general theory predicts; they may find open choice anxiety-provoking and ambiguous rationale confusing. A focused analysis would examine what autonomy support should look like for students at different points on the causality orientations spectrum.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[relatedness-need]]
> > SDT's most undertheorized need deserves its own dialectical examination. Relatedness receives substantially less theoretical development in SDT literature than autonomy (the theory's primary focus) or competence (well-connected to effectance research). Yet the emerging science of belonging, social connection, and perceived partner responsiveness suggests that the relational dimension of motivation is both more complex and more consequential than SDT's standard treatment implies. The connection between SDT's relatedness need and attachment theory, Bowlby's secure base, and belonging uncertainty research would substantially enrich the framework.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[goal-content-theory]]
> > SDT's extension to goal content — distinguishing intrinsic aspirations (personal growth, community contribution, meaningful relationships) from extrinsic aspirations (wealth, fame, physical attractiveness) — applies the needs framework to what people pursue rather than how they pursue it. The [[aspiration-index]] operationalizes this distinction and has generated substantial evidence that intrinsic goal orientation predicts well-being better than goal attainment per se. A dialectical re-examination of GCT would ask: is the intrinsic/extrinsic goal content distinction genuinely universal, or does it reflect specific cultural values about what constitutes meaningful life goals?
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[relationship-motivation-theory]]
> > SDT's most recently elaborated mini-theory applies the basic needs framework to close relationships, arguing that genuinely loving relationships require both partners to experience need satisfaction *within* the relationship rather than simply providing it to each other. This creates interesting predictions: relationships in which one partner provides autonomy support and the other does not are likely to be asymmetrically satisfying in ways that undermine the relationship's quality over time. A focused analysis would connect RMT to attachment theory, interdependence theory, and the growing literature on perceived partner responsiveness.

> [!further-exploration] From: [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29|situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[elaborative-inference]]
> > Inference generation is the mechanistic bridge between text-base processing and situation model construction — it is the cognitive process that this report identified as the proximate cause of situation model failure in specific comprehenders and as the process that must be deliberately cultivated to overcome the Text-Base Trap. A dedicated dialectical re-examination of the inference generation literature — including the bridging/elaborative distinction, the minimal inference hypothesis debate, and training protocols — would be the single highest-value expansion of this report's framework.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Phase III's empirical challenge identified inference generation failure as the mechanism by which intact decoding co-exists with poor situation model construction.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Dialectical Re-Examination (received view: "inference generation is automatic and beyond explicit training")
> > **Prerequisites:** [[situation-model]], [[working-memory-in-reading]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[prior-knowledge]]
> > This report established that prior knowledge is constitutive of situation model construction, not merely facilitative. A dedicated treatment of how background knowledge functions in reading, how knowledge-building strategies can be systematically used to prepare for knowledge-demanding texts, and how the Matthew Effect operates through the knowledge-comprehension coupling would address the most consequential practical implication of this re-examination.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Phase III's critical lens and Phase III's philosophical challenge both converge on prior knowledge as constitutive; this is the most actionable practical finding.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis (question: "How should a reader strategically build the prior knowledge needed to comprehend a target text?")
> > **Prerequisites:** [[schema-theory]], [[advance-organizer]], [[situation-model]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[metacognitive-monitoring]]
> > Phase V's metacognitive inversion requirement — monitoring for situation model coherence in the absence of confusion — demands a sophisticated account of how comprehension monitoring works and how it can be trained. The Metacognitive Monitoring PKB node should be expanded to address specifically reading-level monitoring, the fluency illusion override problem, and empirically validated protocols for detecting situation model failures before they are exposed by external comprehension tests.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** The Text-Base Trap is sustained by monitoring failure; breaking the trap requires developing situation-model-level monitoring capacity.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Dialectical Re-Examination (received view: "comprehension monitoring is automatic and reliable")
> > **Prerequisites:** [[situation-model]], [[the-fluency-trap]], [[metacognitive-calibration]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[matthew-effect-in-reading]]
> > The Matthew Effect deserves a dedicated dialectical re-examination that goes beyond Stanovich's original formulation to engage with subsequent research, criticisms, and the mechanisms through which it operates. The connection to situation model construction established in this report — that knowledge-poor readers cannot bootstrap comprehension through strategic attention because prior knowledge is constitutive — provides a mechanistic account that the original Matthew Effect paper did not supply.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Phase III's critical lens; the Matthew Effect is the population-level manifestation of the situation model's prior-knowledge dependence.
> > **Priority:** High
